docs/04-explanation/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem (1).md:51:Prompt Context Caching: We also implement a runtime cache for frequently needed context. For example, if a certain query (or intent) recurs, we can cache the assembled context from last time. Similarly, if an LLM agent repeatedly asks for a particular document snippet, we avoid re-embedding or re-summarizing it each time by storing its vector and compressed form in memory. This ties into the session intent: we identify high-value context items from recent turns and pre-fetch/cache them for the next turn. All caches are kept in-memory (and optionally persisted via Letta’s working memory tier) with keys like (document_id, chunk_id, version) to ensure idempotency – i.e., if we see the same chunk again with no changes, we reuse the existing prelude and embedding rather than recompute. This saves both latency and token cost (since LLM summarization of preludes consumes tokens). Our pipeline is idempotent at every stage: re-ingesting the same document yields the same chunk outputs; mem.upsert calls use stable IDs so that duplicates are updates, not new nodes.

docs/04-explanation/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem (1).md:120:All mem.upsert and graph.link operations are designed to be idempotent and lightweight. ConPort (which uses SQLite under the hood per workspace ￼) can handle these as simple upsert queries. We batch calls where possible (e.g. upserting all retrieved nodes in one batch API call to reduce overhead). In case ConPort is unavailable (network or DB down), these operations will fail gracefully (we catch exceptions). A feature flag can disable memory logging if needed, buffering the logs locally. Specifically, we implement a buffer-and-retry: if mem.upsert fails, we push that data into an in-memory queue with a timestamp. A background coroutine will retry those operations periodically until they succeed (or log to a file for later reconciliation). This ensures that a temporary outage in the memory subsystem doesn’t break the retrieval flow – the assistant still answers, and we later reconcile the graph state. PII or sensitive data is handled by redaction: if chunks contain credentials or personal info (ideally they shouldn’t in project docs; if so, those should be masked at ingestion), we avoid logging that content in the graph. ConPort is mostly for technical context and decisions, so PII exposure is minimal, but we apply a filter to mem.upsert that scrubs known sensitive patterns (like API keys) to be safe.
docs/04-explanation/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem (1).md:132:Session to Graph Promotions: The chat itself can generate new knowledge that should persist. We implement “promotion rules” that decide when to take information from the conversation and record it in ConPort (the project memory). For instance, if the user explicitly states a decision (“Alright, we’ll use Redis for caching moving forward”), the assistant (or a behind-the-scenes monitor agent) will detect that and call something like mem.upsert(type="Decision", desc="Using Redis for caching", details={...}) as illustrated earlier. Another example: if the user solves a problem through the assistant’s help, the final explanation or fix can be logged as a KnowledgeNote node for future reference (so next time a similar error occurs, the system has that answer stored). We define triggers such as:
docs/04-explanation/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem (1).md:301:	•	Code Updates: We integrate with the version control (Git) hooks: after each merge to main branch, trigger a re-index for affected files. We have a script that diffs the last indexed commit vs new commit: for each changed file, re-chunk and upsert those chunks in Milvus (overwriting old ones). Remove deleted file’s entries. This can be done via Milvus delete by PK for those chunk IDs. Because we used stable chunk IDs based on content or line numbers, we might also just update the content in place if minor changes – but simpler is to delete old chunks of that file and insert new ones, then call mem.upsert to update graph nodes if needed. This ensures the vector store is in sync with latest code. We schedule a nightly full sync as well in case any hook misses (belt-and-suspenders).
docs/04-explanation/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem (1).md:325:	•	ConPort Down: If memory graph is down, the pipeline still works for retrieval (Milvus doesn’t depend on ConPort). We just won’t log or be able to use long-term memory. The system will continue, perhaps notifying that memory features are degraded. All mem.upsert calls are queued (as described) and will be retried when ConPort comes back. The reconcile process ensures no data loss: once back up, the buffered logs are written in order. We also might have an admin script to manually reconcile from logs if needed.

docs/archive/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem.md:63:Prompt Context Caching: We also implement a runtime cache for frequently needed context. For example, if a certain query (or intent) recurs, we can cache the assembled context from last time. Similarly, if an LLM agent repeatedly asks for a particular document snippet, we avoid re-embedding or re-summarizing it each time by storing its vector and compressed form in memory. This ties into the session intent: we identify high-value context items from recent turns and pre-fetch/cache them for the next turn. All caches are kept in-memory (and optionally persisted via Letta’s working memory tier) with keys like (document_id, chunk_id, version) to ensure idempotency – i.e., if we see the same chunk again with no changes, we reuse the existing prelude and embedding rather than recompute. This saves both latency and token cost (since LLM summarization of preludes consumes tokens). Our pipeline is idempotent at every stage: re-ingesting the same document yields the same chunk outputs; mem.upsert calls use stable IDs so that duplicates are updates, not new nodes.

docs/archive/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem.md:132:All mem.upsert and graph.link operations are designed to be idempotent and lightweight. ConPort (which uses SQLite under the hood per workspace ￼) can handle these as simple upsert queries. We batch calls where possible (e.g. upserting all retrieved nodes in one batch API call to reduce overhead). In case ConPort is unavailable (network or DB down), these operations will fail gracefully (we catch exceptions). A feature flag can disable memory logging if needed, buffering the logs locally. Specifically, we implement a buffer-and-retry: if mem.upsert fails, we push that data into an in-memory queue with a timestamp. A background coroutine will retry those operations periodically until they succeed (or log to a file for later reconciliation). This ensures that a temporary outage in the memory subsystem doesn’t break the retrieval flow – the assistant still answers, and we later reconcile the graph state. PII or sensitive data is handled by redaction: if chunks contain credentials or personal info (ideally they shouldn’t in project docs; if so, those should be masked at ingestion), we avoid logging that content in the graph. ConPort is mostly for technical context and decisions, so PII exposure is minimal, but we apply a filter to mem.upsert that scrubs known sensitive patterns (like API keys) to be safe.
docs/archive/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem.md:144:Session to Graph Promotions: The chat itself can generate new knowledge that should persist. We implement “promotion rules” that decide when to take information from the conversation and record it in ConPort (the project memory). For instance, if the user explicitly states a decision (“Alright, we’ll use Redis for caching moving forward”), the assistant (or a behind-the-scenes monitor agent) will detect that and call something like mem.upsert(type="Decision", desc="Using Redis for caching", details={...}) as illustrated earlier. Another example: if the user solves a problem through the assistant’s help, the final explanation or fix can be logged as a KnowledgeNote node for future reference (so next time a similar error occurs, the system has that answer stored). docs/archive/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem.md:313:	•	Code Updates: We integrate with the version control (Git) hooks: after each merge to main branch, trigger a re-index for affected files. We have a script that diffs the last indexed commit vs new commit: for each changed file, re-chunk and upsert those chunks in Milvus (overwriting old ones). Remove deleted file’s entries. This can be done via Milvus delete by PK for those chunk IDs. Because we used stable chunk IDs based on content or line numbers, we might also just update the content in place if minor changes – but simpler is to delete old chunks of that file and insert new ones, then call mem.upsert to update graph nodes if needed. This ensures the vector store is in sync with latest code. We schedule a nightly full sync as well in case any hook misses (belt-and-suspenders).

We also might have an admin script to manually reconcile from logs if needed.
